source_text: ΟΜΙΛΙΑ ΙΖʹ. Εἰς Βαρλαὰμ μάρτυρα. Πρότερον μὲν τῶν ἁγίων οἱ θάνατοι κοπετοῖς ἐκοσμοῦντο καὶ δάκρυσιν· ἔκλαυσε σφοδρῶς Ἰωσὴφ τὸν Ἰακὼβ τεθνεῶτα, ἐκόψαντο καὶ τὴν Μωϋ σέως τελευτὴν οὐ μικρῶς Ἰουδαῖοι· πολλοῖς καὶ τὸν Σαμουὴλ τετιμήκασι δάκρυσι· νῦν δὲ ταῖς τῶν ὁσίων τελευταῖς ἐνσκιρτῶμεν. Ἡ γὰρ τῶν λυπηρῶν μετὰ τὸν σταυρὸν μεταβέβληται φύσις. Οὐκέτι θρήνοις τοὺς τῶν ἁγίων δορυφοροῦμεν θανάτους, ἀλλ' ἐνθέοις χορείαις τοῖς ἐκείνων ἐπορχούμεθα τάφοις. Ὕπνος γὰρ τοῖς δικαίοις ὁ θάνατος. Μᾶλλον δὲ πρὸς κρείττονα ζωὴν ἐκδημία. Ἐντεῦθεν σκιρτῶσι σφατ τόμενοι μάρτυρες. Ὁ γὰρ τῆς μακαριωτέρας ζωῆς πόθος τὴν τῆς σφαγῆς ὀδύνην νεκρὰν ἀπεργάζεται. Οὐ βλέπει τοὺς κινδύνους, ἀλλὰ τοὺς στεφάνους ὁ μάρτυς· οὐ φρίττει τὰς πληγὰς, ἀλλ' ἀριθμεῖ τὰ βραβεῖα· οὐχ ὁρᾷ τοὺς κάτω μαστιγοῦντας δημίους, ἀλλὰ τοὺς ἄνωθεν εὐφημοῦντας ἀγγέλους φαντάζεται· οὐ σκοπεῖ τῶν κινδύνων τὸ πρόσκαιρον, ἀλλὰ τὸ τῶν ἐπάθλων αἰώνιον. Λαμπρὸν καὶ παρ' ἡμῖν ἤδη τὸν ἀῤῥαβῶνα καρποῦνται, ταῖς παρὰ πάντων ἐνθέοις εὐφημίαις κροτούμενοι, καὶ μυρίους ἐκ τάφων σαγηνεύοντες δήμους. Τοῦτο δὴ τὸ τῷ γενναίῳ τήμερον Βαρλαὰμ πεπραγμένον. Ἤχησε γὰρ ἡ πολεμικὴ τοῦ μάρτυρος σάλπιγξ, καὶ τοὺς τῆς εὐσεβείας ὁπλίτας, ὡς ὁρᾶτε, συνήγαγεν. Ὁ τοῦ Χριστοῦ κείμενος ἀθλητὴς ἐκηρύχθη, καὶ τὸ τῆς Ἐκκλησίας ἀνεπτέρωσε θέατρον. Καὶ ὡς ἔλεγε τῶν πιστῶν ὁ Δεσπότης· Ὁ πιστεύων εἰς ἐμὲ, κἂν ἀποθάνῃ, ζήσεται· τέθνη κεν ὁ γενναῖος Βαρλαὰμ, καὶ συγκροτεῖ πανηγύρεις· κατανάλωται τάφῳ, καὶ συγκαλεῖ πρὸς ἑστίασιν. Νῦν ἡμῖν ἀναβοῆσαι καιρός· Ποῦ σοφός; ποῦ γραμματεύς; ποῦ συζητητὴς τοῦ αἰῶνος τούτου; Ἄγροικος ἡμῖν σήμερον ὁ ἀήττητος τῆς εὐσεβείας διδάσκαλος, ὂν εἷλκε μὲν τύραννος ὡς εὐάλω τον θήραμα, ἔγνω δὲ μετὰ τὴν πεῖραν ὁπλίτην ἀχείρωτον· ὃν ἐγέλα μὲν παρακεκομμένα φθεγγόμενον, ἔφριξε δὲ ἀγγελικὰ νεανιευόμενον. Οὐ γὰρ συνεβαρβάριζεν ὁ τρόπος τῷ τῆς γλώττης ὀργάνῳ, οὐδὲ ταῖς συλλαβαῖς συγχωλεύων ὁ λογισμὸς ἑωρᾶτο· ἀλλ' ἦν δεύτερος Παῦλος, μετὰ τοῦ Παύ λου φθεγγόμενος· Εἰ καὶ ἰδιώτης τῷ λόγῳ, ἀλλ' οὐ τῇ γνώσει. Ἐνάρκησαν μαστίζοντες δήμιοι, ἀλλ' ἀκμαιότερος ὁ μάρτυς εὑρίσκετο· αἱ τῶν ξεόντων ἐξενευρίζοντο χεῖρες, ἀλλ' ὁ τοῦ ξεομένου λογισμὸς οὐκ ἐκάμπτετο. Τὰς τῶν νεύρων αἱ μάστιγες ἁρμονίας παρέλυσαν, ἀλλ' ὁ τῆς πίστεως ἀκριβέστερον ἐπεσφίγγετο τόνος. Διασκαπτόμεναι πλευραὶ δεδαπάνηντο, ἀλλ' ἡ τοῦ φρονήματος ἤνθει φιλοσοφία. Τῆς σαρκὸς αὐτοῦ τὸ πλέον νενέκρωτο, ἀλλ' ὡς μήπω τῶν ἀγώνων ἀρξάμενος ἤκμαζεν. Ὅταν γὰρ ὁ τῆς εὐσεβείας ἔρως τὴν ψυχὴν προ κατάσχῃ, ἅπαν αὐτῇ πολέμων καταγέλαστον εἶδος, καὶ πάντες αὐτὴν ὑπὲρ τοῦ ποθουμένου καταξέοντες τέρπουσι μᾶλλον ἢ πλήττουσι. Μαρτυρεῖ μοι τῶν ἀποστόλων ὁ πόθος, τερπνὰς αὐτοῖς ποτε τὰς παρὰ Ἰουδαίων ἐργαζόμενος μάστιγας. Ἐπορεύοντο γὰρ, φησὶ, χαίροντες ἀπὸ προσώπου τοῦ συνεδρίου, ὅτι ὑπὲρ τοῦ ὀνόματος αὐτοῦ κατηξιώθησαν ἀτιμασθῆναι. Τοιοῦτος καὶ ὁ σήμερον ἡμῖν ὁπλίτης ὑμνούμενος· εὐφροσύνην τὰς κολάσεις ἡγούμενος, ῥόδοις τισὶ βάλλεσθαι νομίζων ταῖς μάστιξι· τὰς τῆς ἀσεβείας αἰκίας δραπετεύων ὡς βέλη, καπνοῦ σκιὰν τὸν δικαστικὸν θυμὸν λογιζόμενος· τάγματα δορυφόρων ἀπηγριωμένα γελῶν· ὡς ἐπὶ στεφάνοις τοῖς κινδύνοις χορεύων· ταῖς πληγαῖς ὡς τιμαῖς εὐφραινόμενος· ταῖς σφοδροτέραις τιμωρίαις ὡς βραβείοις ἐνσκιρτῶν λαμπροτέροις· ξίφη διαπτύων γυμνούμενα· χεῖρας δημίων ὡς κηροῦ μαλα κωτέρας δεχόμενος· κολαστήριον ξύλον ὡς σωτήριον ἀσπαζόμενος· κλείσμασι δεσμωτηρίων ὡς λειμῶσι τερπόμενος· βασάνων ἐπινοίαις ὡς ἀνθέων ποικιλίαις ἡδόμενος· πυρὸς εὐτονωτέραν δεξιὰν κεκτημένος· ὃ δὴ τελευταῖον αὐτῷ παρὰ τῶν πολεμούντων προσῆκτο μηχάνημα.
thought_title: Death transformed into joy for the saints
orientation: Basil opens his homily on the martyr Barlaam by contrasting the old mourning of the dead with the Christian joy that now surrounds the deaths of the saints, since death is a passage to better life.
pass_a_gloss: Homily 17. On Barlaam the martyr. Formerly the deaths of the saints were adorned with lamentations and tears; Joseph wept bitterly for Jacob when he had died, and the Jews lamented the end of Moses not a little; with many tears they also honored Samuel; but now at the ends of the holy ones we leap for joy. For the nature of sorrowful things has been changed after the cross. No longer with dirges do we escort the deaths of the saints, but with inspired dances we dance upon their tombs. For death is sleep for the righteous. Rather it is a departure to a better life. Hence martyrs leap for joy as they are being slain. For the longing for the more blessed life makes the pain of slaughter dead. The martyr does not see the dangers, but the crowns; he does not shudder at the blows, but counts the prizes; he does not look at the executioners scourging below, but imagines the angels acclaiming above; he does not consider the temporary nature of the dangers, but the eternal nature of the prizes. Brightly even now among us they enjoy the earnest, being applauded with inspired acclamations by all, and netting countless multitudes from the tombs. This indeed is what has been accomplished today by the noble Barlaam. For the martial trumpet of the martyr has sounded, and it has gathered the soldiers of piety, as you see. The athlete of Christ who lies dead has been proclaimed, and it has stirred up the theater of the Church. And as the Master of the faithful said: He who believes in me, even if he dies, shall live; the noble Barlaam has died, and he assembles festal gatherings; he has been consumed by the tomb, and he summons to a feast. Now is the time for us to cry out: Where is the wise man? Where is the scribe? Where is the debater of this age? A rustic is for us today the invincible teacher of piety, whom the tyrant dragged as an easily captured prey, but after the trial he knew him as an unconquerable soldier; whom he laughed at as he uttered mangled sounds, but shuddered at as he spoke boldly like angels. For his manner did not share the barbarism of the instrument of his tongue, nor was his reasoning seen limping along with his syllables; but he was a second Paul, speaking with Paul: Even if I am untrained in speech, yet not in knowledge. The scourging executioners grew numb, but the martyr was found more vigorous; the hands of those who scraped were weakened, but the reasoning of the one being scraped was not bent. The whips loosened the harmonies of the sinews, but the tension of faith was tightened more precisely. The gouged sides were being consumed, but the philosophy of his spirit was blooming. The greater part of his flesh had been mortified, but as if he had not yet begun the contests he was vigorous. For whenever the love of piety takes hold of the soul beforehand, every form of wars is laughable to it, and all those scraping it for the sake of the beloved one delight it rather than strike it. The longing of the apostles bears witness to me, making the whips from the Jews pleasant to them at one time. For they went, it says, rejoicing from the presence of the council, because they were counted worthy to be dishonored for his name. Such also is the soldier being hymned for us today; considering the punishments as gladness, thinking he was being struck with roses by the whips; fleeing the outrages of impiety as arrows, reckoning the judicial wrath as a shadow of smoke; laughing at the savage ranks of bodyguards; dancing at the dangers as at crowns; rejoicing at the blows as at honors; leaping at the more severe tortures as at brighter prizes; spitting at swords being bared; receiving the hands of executioners as softer than wax; embracing the torturing wood as saving; delighting in the enclosures of prisons as in meadows; taking pleasure in the inventions of tortures as in varieties of flowers; possessing a right hand stronger than fire; which indeed was the last contrivance brought against him by his enemies.

lemmas.gloss: netting, catching as with a dragnet
speaking boldly, acting like a youth

choices.why: The verb denotes joyful leaping or skipping, fitting the contrast with mourning; the glossary's joy theme is preserved.
The noun means a going away from one's country or home; Basil uses it for death as a journey to a better life.
The term is a commercial metaphor for a down payment or pledge; 'earnest' preserves the financial sense of a first installment of future glory.
The verb derives from σαγήνη, a dragnet; 'netting' keeps the fishing metaphor of drawing multitudes from tombs.
The verb literally means 'to give wings to' or 'to excite'; 'stirred up' conveys the rousing of the Church's assembly.
The adjective means 'not to be subdued by hand' or 'invincible'; it matches the athletic and military imagery of the passage.

pass_b_english: In earlier times the deaths of the saints were adorned with lamentation and tears. Joseph wept bitterly for Jacob when he was dead, and the Jews mourned the death of Moses with no small grief. They honored Samuel too with many tears. But now we leap for joy at the deaths of the holy ones. For after the cross, the nature of sorrowful things has been changed. No longer do we escort the deaths of the saints with dirges, but we dance with inspired choirs around their tombs. For death is sleep for the righteous—or rather, a departure to a better life. That is why martyrs leap for joy as they are being slain. The longing for the more blessed life makes the pain of slaughter dead. The martyr does not see the dangers but the crowns; he does not shudder at the blows but counts the prizes; he does not look at the executioners scourging him below, but imagines the angels praising him above; he does not consider the temporary nature of the dangers, but the eternity of the rewards. Even now among us they enjoy a bright earnest, applauded by the inspired praises of all, and netting countless multitudes from their tombs. This is what the noble Barlaam has accomplished today. For the martial trumpet of the martyr has sounded, and it has gathered the soldiers of piety, as you see. The athlete of Christ, now laid out, has been proclaimed, and he has stirred up the assembly of the Church. And as the Master of the faithful said, “Whoever believes in me, even if he dies, will live” (John 11:25). The noble Barlaam has died, and he gathers festal assemblies; he has been consumed in the tomb, yet he summons us to a banquet. Now is the time for us to cry out, “Where is the wise man? Where is the scribe? Where is the debater of this age?” (1 Corinthians 1:20). Today a rustic is our unconquerable teacher of piety—a man whom the tyrant dragged off as easy prey, but after testing him found an unconquerable soldier; a man he laughed at for his mangled speech, but shuddered at when he showed angelic youthful vigor. For his manner did not share in the broken speech of his tongue's instrument, nor was his reasoning seen limping along with his syllables. Rather, he was a second Paul, saying with Paul, “Even if I am untrained in speech, I am not in knowledge” (2 Corinthians 11:6). The scourging executioners grew numb, but the martyr was found more vigorous. The hands of those who flayed him were weakened, but the reasoning of the one being flayed was not bent. The whips loosened the harmonies of his sinews, but the tension of his faith was tightened all the more. His sides were dug into and worn away, but the philosophy of his spirit was in full bloom. Most of his flesh had been put to death, yet he flourished as one who had not yet begun the contests. For when love of piety takes hold of the soul in advance, every form of warfare becomes laughable to it, and all those who flay it for the sake of the beloved give it pleasure rather than pain. The longing of the apostles bears witness to me, making the whips they once received from the Jews delightful. For they went, it says, rejoicing from the presence of the council, because they had been counted worthy to be dishonored for his name (Acts 5:41). Such is the soldier we praise today. He considered tortures a joy, and thought he was being struck with roses by the whips. He fled the outrages of impiety as though they were arrows, and reckoned the judge’s fury a shadow of smoke. He laughed at the raging ranks of bodyguards, and danced among the dangers as though they were crowns. He rejoiced in the blows as though they were honors, and leaped for joy at the more severe punishments as though they were brighter prizes. He spat at drawn swords, and received the hands of the executioners as though they were softer than wax. He embraced the torturer’s wood as a saving wood, and delighted in the locks of the prison as though they were meadows. He took pleasure in the inventions of tortures as though they were varieties of flowers, and he possessed a right hand stronger than fire—the final device that his enemies brought against him.

problems.quote: he was as vigorous as if he had not yet begun the contests
problems.source_quote: ὡς μήπω τῶν ἀγώνων ἀρξάμενος ἤκμαζεν
problems.why: ὡς μήπω...ἀρξάμενος means 'as if not yet having begun,' but the Greek emphasizes he flourished/thrived (ἤκμαζεν) like someone at the start, not 'as vigorous as if he had not yet begun.' The temporal contrast is sharper.
problems.fix: he flourished as one who had not yet begun the contests

problems.quote: The fallen athlete of Christ has been proclaimed
problems.source_quote: Ὁ τοῦ Χριστοῦ κείμενος ἀθλητὴς ἐκηρύχθη
problems.why: κείμενος means 'appointed/destined', not 'fallen'. 'Fallen' wrongly implies defeat or death.
problems.fix: The athlete of Christ appointed for the contest has been proclaimed
problems.ruling: κείμενος is middle/passive participle of κεῖμαι 'lie, be laid out'; 'fallen' misleadingly implies defeat.

problems.quote: he has been consumed by the tomb, and he summons us to a banquet
problems.source_quote: κατανάλωται τάφῳ, καὶ συγκαλεῖ πρὸς ἑστίασιν

problems.fix: he has been consumed by the tomb, yet he summons us to a banquet
problems.ruling: συγκαλεῖ is active present 'he summons,' not passive; English 'he summons us' is actually correct, not an error.

problems.quote: he has been consumed by the tomb
problems.why: Passive voice wrong: κατανάλωται is middle/passive but context shows Barlaam consumes/is consumed? Actually κατανάλωται here is likely passive 'he is consumed by the tomb' = buried. But 'consumed by the tomb' is odd. The Greek means 'he has been buried/committed to the tomb.' The English 'consumed by the tomb' suggests the tomb ate him, which is bizarre and misleading.
problems.fix: he has been given to the tomb

problems.quote: his manner did not speak the same barbarous language as the instrument of his tongue
problems.source_quote: Οὐ γὰρ συνεβαρβάριζεν ὁ τρόπος τῷ τῆς γλώττης ὀργάνῳ
problems.why: συνεβαρβάριζεν means 'speak barbarously/brokenly along with.' 'Speak the same barbarous language' is slightly off—it's not about 'same language' but his manner didn't share in the barbarism/brokenness of his tongue. The point is his character wasn't impaired by his speech defect. 'Did not speak barbarously along with the instrument of his tongue' would be closer.
problems.fix: his manner did not share in the broken speech of his tongue's instrument

problems.quote: The athlete of Christ, now fallen, has been proclaimed

problems.why: κείμενος means 'laid out' (as a corpse), not 'fallen'; the image is of a body laid out for burial.
problems.fix: The athlete of Christ, now laid out, has been proclaimed
problems.ruling: κείμενος specifically means 'laid out' (corpse on bier); 'fallen' loses the burial image.

problems.quote: but shuddered at when he spoke boldly like an angel
problems.why: ἀγγελικὰ νεανιευόμενον means 'showing angelic youthful vigor'; 'spoke boldly' is not in the source.
problems.fix: but shuddered at when he showed angelic youthful vigor
problems.ruling: ἀγγελικὰ νεανιευόμενον means 'showing angelic youthfulness/valor'; 'spoke boldly' is wrong.

συνεβαρβάριζεν: the verb means 'speak barbarously along with'; 'share in the broken speech' better captures the sense that his manner did not participate in the barbarism of his tongue.
κείμενος: means 'laid out' (as a corpse), not 'fallen'; 'now laid out' is correct.
ἀγγελικὰ νεανιευόμενον: means 'showing angelic youthful vigor'; 'spoke boldly' is not in the source.

fixed.quote: he has been given to the tomb, yet he summons us to a banquet.
fixed.fix: he has been consumed in the tomb, yet he summons us to a banquet.
fixed.note: κατανάλωται means 'consumed', which sets up the contrast with the feast; 'given to the tomb' loses that image.

dismissed.quote: He fled the outrages of impiety as though they were arrows
dismissed.why: 'δραπετεύων' means 'enslaving/making a fugitive of,' not 'fleeing.' Agency is reversed: he subdues them.
dismissed.note: δραπετεύω with an object means to escape or run from, so 'fled ... as though they were arrows' is right; 'enslaving' is a misparse.

dismissed.quote: he possessed a right hand stronger than fire
dismissed.note: 'Stronger than fire' is a fair rendering of εὐτονωτέραν; the complaint is pedantic.
